increment: savepoint-hardening: make the provider sync unit atomic in its own right
evaluator: fresh independent Level 2 evaluator on a live Postgres stack; the S4 close-out owns the F008 passes flip
approval_notes: Orchestrator-directed follow-up to PR #40 (merged as f790633), which closed the sync_coverage() prune defect and made the Q9-A evidence floor a DATABASE invariant via _assert_persisted_coverage_floor() / CoverageFloorError.

THE GAP. PR #40's 'the erosion never commits' guarantee is a property of the CALLERS, not of the code. sync_coverage() only flush()es (the caller owns the transaction -- a documented invariant since F005 slice 1); its sole non-test caller is sync_provider (config_sync.py:695), whose sole caller is runner.py:272, which sits OUTSIDE any try/except; and runner.py's CLI is a bare 'with Session(engine)' + session.commit() after the loop. A future caller shaped 'try: sync_provider(...) except Exception: continue' followed by a commit WOULD persist the erosion, because the DELETEs and the partial writes are already flushed into the transaction.

WHY NOW. runner.py already uses exactly that per-source savepoint + continue shape at lines ~296 and ~341, and Wave 3 adds six providers on this path, so a batch runner of that shape is the expected next step rather than a hypothetical. The merged docs state the caveat honestly and point at this work.

SCOPE IS THE PROVIDER UNIT, NOT THE COVERAGE BLOCK -- load-bearing. A coverage-block-only savepoint CREATES the problem it aims to prevent: on a NEW provider's first sync there is no prior coverage to revert to, so it would commit a provider with ZERO coverage rows; every category then reads 'unknown', and _assert_persisted_coverage_floor returns early on 'not checked' so nothing detects it. That is strictly worse than today's whole-transaction abort, and 'six new providers, first sync' is a literal description of Wave 3. Provider-unit scope makes the unit coherent: fully synced or entirely untouched, never provider-without-coverage.

rollback() then raise -- NEVER rollback() then return. Returning a half-built SyncResult would REPORT SUCCESS for a sync that did not happen: a fresh silent-degradation vector. (It would remain readable, since SyncResult holds primitive ids and dataclasses rather than ORM objects -- which is what makes it dangerous rather than merely broken.) The exception type is not swallowed or translated: CoverageFloorError must still reach the caller as itself, and a rollback that itself fails must not displace it.
NO MIGRATION. Alembic head stays 0011_provider_category_coverage, single head. No new runtime or test dependency, no Redis, no FTS, no live network, no credentialed provider API, no secrets.

The regression test is the part that is easy to write dishonestly. The integration 'session' fixture binds to a connection inside an outer transaction that teardown rolls back, so a test written against it would PASS even if the property broke -- decoration, not enforcement, and worse than no test because it manufactures false confidence. The test therefore takes its own engine, performs a real commit(), reads back on a SEPARATE connection, and tears down explicitly.

The test uses a UNIQUE provider slug it creates and destroys itself, never 'cloudflare'. The hazard is slug collision, not self-inflicted cascade: committing under 'cloudflare' shares a row with every other test and fixture in that database, and an offer_version row created by an unrelated test would block the teardown cascade intermittently depending on execution order. A unique slug makes the teardown safe by construction.
objective: Make the four writes of sync_provider() -- provider row, source rows, categorise_services(), sync_coverage() -- one atomic unit that either fully lands or leaves the database entirely untouched, by wrapping them in a SAVEPOINT that rolls back and RE-RAISES on any failure. This converts PR #40's 'the erosion never commits' from a property of the current call chain into a property of the code itself, so a caller shaped 'try: sync_provider(...) except Exception: continue' followed by a commit -- the shape runner.py already uses per source, and the expected shape of a Wave-3 batch runner -- cannot persist a half-synced provider. Then PIN that property with a regression test that commits for real against its own engine and reads back on a separate connection, so a future caller that breaks it goes RED rather than silently degrading.
scope: apps/api/app/ingest/config_sync.py: sync_provider() opens session.begin_nested() around ALL FOUR writes (the provider row, every source row, categorise_services() and sync_coverage()), commits the savepoint on success, and on ANY exception rolls the savepoint back and re-raises the original exception unchanged. The scope is deliberately the whole provider unit rather than the coverage block alone, for the new-provider reason in the approval notes.

apps/api/app/ingest/config_sync.py: docstring updates on sync_provider() and the module header recording the new atomicity guarantee in exactly the terms implemented -- the unit is all-or-nothing WITHIN the caller's transaction, the caller still owns the transaction and this still never commits it, and the exception still propagates so a caller that ignores it learns nothing new.

tests/integration/test_ingest_sync_savepoint.py (new file): the CLI-shape regression test. Its own engine, a real commit(), read-back on a separate connection, explicit teardown, and a unique per-run provider slug materialised as a real YAML file loaded through load_and_validate() so the 14-slug and Q9-A floor validators are genuinely exercised. Two tests: (a) a failing sync whose exception the caller SWALLOWS and then commits must leave zero provider / source / coverage rows for that slug; (b) the happy path must still commit all of the provider, its sources and its fourteen coverage rows, so the savepoint is proven not to swallow good writes.

AMENDMENT (made during implementation, before the PR): docs/DATA_MODEL.md and docs/PROVIDER_ADAPTERS.md each carry a paragraph added by PR #40 stating that the no-commit guarantee is 'a property of the callers, not yet of sync_coverage itself' and that a provider-unit savepoint is 'tracked as a follow-up'. This change makes both sentences false, so they are rewritten to describe exactly what is implemented and nothing more. Leaving them would be a stale claim in the repository; widening them beyond the implementation is what failed a previous PR twice, so the new text names the savepoint, its provider-unit scope, the re-raise, and the unchanged caller-owns-the-transaction rule -- and claims nothing else.

AMENDMENT 2 (remediation of the Level-2 FAIL on PR #41; findings F-1..F-4, criteria 1/3/4/5 confirmed PASS and NOT reworked). F-1: savepoint.rollback() could itself raise (ResourceClosedError on an already-closed nested transaction) and displace the primary exception, because the bare 'raise' was only reached if the rollback succeeded. The rollback is now wrapped in its own try/except; a secondary failure is attached to the original exception via add_note() (with the observed savepoint.is_active value) rather than discarded or propagated, so the caller always receives the original exception unchanged in type AND identity. Note the rollback is still ATTEMPTED unconditionally rather than gated on savepoint.is_active: that flag is also False for a nested transaction the failure merely deactivated, which still needs its SAVEPOINT released -- is_active is recorded for diagnosis instead of used as a guard. F-2: the fixture teardown deleted by 'slug LIKE <prefix>%' and asserted zero leftovers by that same predicate, so it could delete a foreign row AND pass its own self-satisfying check. Teardown now captures the provider id and its source ids first and deletes strictly by those ids, and the leftover assertion counts by the captured ids -- a predicate independent of the delete. Probe.committed_counts() likewise counts sources through provider_id rather than by slug prefix. The 'safe by construction' docstring is replaced by one that separates the two properties honestly: slug uniqueness prevents collision, ownership-scoped deletion prevents deleting rows the fixture did not create. F-3: the suite pinned only the coverage axis, so narrowing 'except BaseException' to 'except CoverageFloorError' left the whole live suite green. A third test now injects a sentinel exception (_SentinelSourceWriteError, deliberately unrelated to CoverageFloorError) from the SECOND source write -- after the provider row and the first source have already been flushed -- and asserts {provider:0, source:0, coverage:0} after a swallow-and-commit. A fourth test constructs the inactive-savepoint case for F-1 directly. F-4: the module header, the sync_provider docstring and both documents claimed the guarantee holds 'on any failure'; every such sentence is narrowed to 'whenever any of the four writes raises', with the rollback-failure caveat stated explicitly in DATA_MODEL.md. The docstring's rationale for not returning after a rollback was also factually WRONG -- it claimed the SyncResult is built over ORM objects the rollback expires, when in fact it holds primitive ids and dataclasses and stays readable after commit. The conclusion (never return) is unchanged; the reason is corrected to the honest one: it would report success for a sync that did not happen.

AMENDMENT 3 (round r2, after the r1 independent Level-2 evaluation returned FAIL with findings F-5, F-6, F-7; F-2 and F-3 were confirmed CLOSED by that evaluation and are untouched, as is the unconditional-rollback is_active reasoning, which the evaluator upheld empirically). F-5: exc.add_note() is itself virtually dispatched and therefore attacker-controlled in exactly the way savepoint.rollback() was; a RuntimeError subclass whose add_note() raised, combined with a failing rollback, delivered the note-failure to the caller instead of the original exception. The add_note() call is now wrapped in a bare 'except BaseException: pass'. Silently discarding is correct rather than lazy at this depth: the note exists only to preserve a secondary diagnostic, and once attaching it fails there is no remaining channel to report the tertiary failure through, so the only choice left is between discarding it and letting it displace the primary exception -- which is the very defect being fixed. The savepoint.is_active read was moved inside the same guard, so the set of statements in the except block is closed structurally rather than by inspection. F-6: mutation M5 ('except BaseException' -> 'except Exception') left the suite green while a genuine BaseException raised from categorise_services() -- the third write -- let a caller commit a partial {provider:1, source:3, coverage:0}. The implementation was already correct on that axis; only the pin was missing. A new test raises _SentinelBaseException(BaseException) (deliberately NOT an Exception subclass) from the categorisation write, covering the untested third write and the untested BaseException breadth together. F-7: three stale strings corrected -- the identity claim (falsified until F-5 landed, now true and re-read in its strongest reading), a test assertion message still citing the 'expired ORM objects' rationale that was replaced everywhere else in r1, and the module docstring's literally false claim that 'each test' performs a real commit, which the two rollback-failure tests do not. CLOSED-SET ENUMERATION (required by the r1 report): after F-5 the except block contains exactly four statements that can raise -- (1) the savepoint.is_active read, now inside the rollback guard; (2) the guarded savepoint.rollback(); (3) the guarded exc.add_note(), whose f-string argument also invokes rollback_exc.__repr__ and is therefore covered by the same guard; and (4) the bare 'raise', which re-raises the active exception and introduces nothing new. (1)-(3) are all inside guards that cannot propagate; (4) cannot introduce a different exception. There is therefore no remaining masking path inside sync_provider, and a future round proposing one must show which of these four statements it originates from.

AMENDMENT 4 (round r3, after the r2 independent Level-2 evaluation returned FAIL with a single finding, F-8; F-5 and F-6 were confirmed CLOSED and the four-raise-site closed-set enumeration was audited and confirmed COMPLETE, so that axis is closed permanently and is untouched here). F-8 is earlier than the exception handler: savepoint.commit() successfully issues RELEASE SAVEPOINT and only then does after_transaction_end event dispatch raise, by which point the four writes belong to the caller's enclosing transaction and sync_provider -- which does not own that transaction -- can no longer revert them. The remedy was measured on real PostgreSQL rather than reasoned about, with the caller holding its own unrelated flushed work. Result: every PUBLIC remedy (Session.rollback, get_transaction().rollback, invalidate, close) leaves the caller's commit() succeeding SILENTLY -- changing what persists but not what the caller believes -- and additionally destroys the caller's own unrelated rows, trading a narrow bounded boundary for unbounded loss in the caller's scope. Only writing the PRIVATE SessionTransaction._state / _rollback_exception pair produces a loud PendingRollbackError, and that was rejected for consistency with the earlier refusal to depend on SQLAlchemy internals for is_active: that was a read of a property, this would be a write faking an internal state-machine transition, which a rename would break SILENTLY with no test going red until someone registered a listener. SQLAlchemy 2.0.36 exposes no supported deactivation route -- 'rollback_only' exists only as a join_transaction_mode value for externally-supplied connections, not as a session-level flag. Narrowing the window is structurally impossible because the dangerous step is the terminating one by definition. Owning the transaction outright would solve rather than report, but inverts the caller-owns-the-transaction invariant held since F005 slice 1 and breaks runner.py's per-source savepoints, so it is recorded as rejected-on-blast-radius rather than omitted. The chosen response is therefore to DOCUMENT the boundary honestly and TEST it, not to guard it: the module header, the sync_provider docstring, DATA_MODEL.md and PROVIDER_ADAPTERS.md now state that atomicity covers failures in the four writes and that a failure during SAVEPOINT release is outside it, naming the concrete consequence (a sync reported as failed can still be committed as complete). A new test asserts the DOCUMENTED outcome rather than an aspirational 0/0/0, with a docstring stating explicitly that it pins a boundary and not a guarantee so a passing run cannot later be misread as proof of atomicity in that window; it also pins that the boundary sits exactly at the release, so a failable step slid after savepoint.commit() by a future refactor shows up there. A second test converts the materiality finding into an enforced invariant by scanning apps/ for after_transaction_end / after_transaction_create REGISTRATIONS -- matching the event.listen(...) and @event.listens_for(...) spellings rather than the bare event name, because a name-only scan fires on the documentation of this very boundary and would be silenced or deleted within a round. The trade is disclosed in the test docstring: a dynamically-constructed event name would evade it. Verified by planting both registration spellings and confirming each goes RED, and by mutation M7 (asserting 0/0/0 in place of the documented outcome), which goes RED and so shows the boundary test reads real committed state rather than being vacuous.
out_of_scope: Any migration. Head stays 0011_provider_category_coverage, single head.

runner.py: no refactor, no new batch runner, no change to the existing per-source / per-publish savepoints. The point of the provider-unit savepoint is that a future batch runner becomes correct without runner.py changing today.

migrations/, agent-state/feature_list.json, agent-state/evaluation.json, apps/api/app/ingest/adapters/** (the Wave-3 registration seam must stay byte-stable), apps/web/, apps/api/app/read_api/taxonomy.py and all dependency manifests: zero diff versus main.
Flipping any passes flag. F008 stays passes:false; the S4 close-out owns that.

The four other tracked evaluator observations (B staleness masking a withdrawal, C a (verified_free, unknown) pair staying silent, D contradiction-reader fragility, E _applied_revisions asserting the script graph).
Opportunistic cleanup of anything the work happens to expose: disclosed in the PR body rather than fixed inline.
acceptance_criteria: 1. sync_provider() is atomic in its own right: when any of its four writes raises, the savepoint is rolled back so the provider row, the source rows, the service categorisations and the coverage rows this call produced are all absent from the enclosing transaction -- even if the caller swallows the exception and commits.

2. The failure is never converted into a successful-looking return. sync_provider() re-raises the ORIGINAL exception, unchanged in type and identity; CoverageFloorError reaches the caller as CoverageFloorError with its message intact, and a rollback that itself fails is attached as a note rather than replacing it.

3. The happy path is byte-for-byte unchanged in behaviour: the same SyncResult, the same counts, the same idempotent second run reporting zero changes, and the writes genuinely persist through a real commit().

4. The regression test cannot pass on a rolled-back fixture: it uses its own engine, commits for real, and reads back on a connection it opens separately, so the assertion measures the DATABASE rather than the session's identity map.

5. The regression test is self-cleaning AND ownership-scoped: it operates on a unique per-run provider slug, removes its own provider, source and coverage rows by captured row id (never by slug prefix) in a teardown that runs even when the test body fails, verifies the result by a predicate independent of the delete, and leaves any foreign row untouched.

6. Alembic head is still 0011_provider_category_coverage and single; migrations/, agent-state/feature_list.json, agent-state/evaluation.json, apps/api/app/ingest/adapters/**, apps/web/, apps/api/app/read_api/taxonomy.py and every dependency manifest are byte-identical to main.

risks: A savepoint scoped to the coverage block instead of the provider unit would commit a provider with zero coverage rows on a new provider's first sync -- strictly worse than today. Mitigated by scoping to the whole unit and by acceptance criterion 1 naming all four writes.

Returning a half-built SyncResult after a rollback would report success for a sync that did not happen. (Note: the SyncResult holds primitive ids and dataclasses, so it stays readable after the rollback -- that is what makes returning it dangerous rather than merely broken. An earlier draft of this contract claimed it was built over expired ORM objects; that was inaccurate and is corrected here.) Mitigated by the rollback-then-raise constraint and by mutation probe 2, which pins it.

A test written against the integration 'session' fixture would pass even if the property broke, because that fixture never commits. Mitigated by the dedicated-engine + real-commit + separate-connection design and by mutation probe 1, which must observe a COMMITTED row.

Committing to the shared database risks slug collision and an intermittent, order-dependent teardown failure. Mitigated by a unique per-run slug and an explicit teardown that runs on failure, and verified empirically rather than argued.

SQLAlchemy nesting: sync_provider may be called by a caller that has already opened its own savepoint (the existing floor tests do exactly this). begin_nested() nests correctly, but the existing live suite is the oracle and must stay green.
contract_review: Written BEFORE implementation, per the coding-agent instructions. Amended rather than deviated from silently if the work forces a change; every deviation, edit to a pre-existing test, carve-out and unverifiable claim is disclosed in the PR body.
